💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks.
  • It’s not like the site has simply sat all that time.
  • Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.

It’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped new features, particularly since 2024, but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage.

Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the fresh v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

Sources indicate that first and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

In a recent development, for example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB).

I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits:.

For years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a new terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention promptly. Very happy here.

It has been revealed that oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

It has been revealed that the previous theme had a fairly nice “flat” structure — very few partial directories and most things all in the same top-level source. Totally cool. But an organization nut like me (you should see my house) has to have a place for everything to live. It ain’t perfect, but I’m happy with what I was able to put together without leveling the building in the process.

Recent findings suggest that there are some compromises. Like, /header should really be in /layout. The ordering is really important, though, and some of my ideals were simply not possible. I’m hoping to eventually work in some sort of Cascade Layers structure.

I’m pleased as punch to see the overall size of CSS drop in the process. It went from 180 KB (31.7 KB) to 169 KB (24.6 KB). Not hugely significant, but not not significant either. I had to do a couple tricky things to cheat my way there, like serving all the form styles I’m about to talk about into a separate forms.css file and serving it just on pages where WooCommerce, Restrict Content Pro, and Gravity Forms are enqueued.

Are you starting to notice a trend? We’re still talking about fairly invisible work. CSS-Tricks has so many nooks and crannies that it’s nearly impossible to make things perfectly consistent across the board. But because of those nooks and crannies, so many fixed values, magic numbers, one-off styles, and older utilities were hiding about. I decided to tackle a good chunk of that while reorganizing the Sass.

For example, there are now semantic design tokens that abstract away one-off colors. So many grays, let me tell you. Now there’s a maintainable palette that’s referenced throughout. Same with fonts, font styles, and font sizes. Same with paddings and margins. It feels a lot better to make a change at the “system” level with confidence that the change is taking effect everywhere it needs to.

But this is also where some clearly visible changes happened! Most notably, link styles are consistent all over the place with a small handful of intended and maintained variations. Not only is it more pleasing visually, but it improves accessibility throughout because the inherited styles default to proper visual cues that do not rely solely on color or opacity changes.

Oh, and my favorite piece of this? Forms and tables have both been redone. That’s tough to do in a WordPress theme where these components don’t always come from one source. For example, forms could come from any one of the Gravity Forms, WooCommerce, or Restrict Content Pro plugins, and they all have their own stylesheets. Resetting those allowed me to bring a certain level of harmony in all those instances.

Industry observers note that OK, something even more visual. This is the first time CSS-Tricks has had more than one color scheme! It certainly could have been done a long time ago, but I’d also argue that the design hasn’t really called for a light/dark toggle over the last 8 years or so. It’s a nice blend of both light and dark elements that marry the best of both worlds no matter your theme preference.

Industry observers note that but I had to take a stab, right? The site has predominantly been dark despite the content being against a white background, so I treated things as though a “dark” mode already existed. The result is a creamy light theme that is largely just a change in background and component styles. And I used some of what I learned from the recent “toggle” debate to handle system, dark, and light themes with a single toggle.

What hasn’t changed is the main content container you see in things like articles. That was already white, even in a “dark” mode, and I’m not confident that simply toggling it between white and black is the best approach. Something on the radar for sure.

Oh, and it’s all wired up to a view transition that slides the newly introduced theme over the previous one.

I hope you think the site’s header and footer are cute. Yes, cute. That’s what I was going for when adding a colorful series of dots as the backdrop.

It has been revealed that sorta like a subtle candy texture, right? Or a colorful group of stars? I dunno, but I’m calling it “Jawbreaker” for lack of a better term and because it reminds me of the jawbreaker candy I loved as a kid. Naming still sucks.

It’s all part of the same SVG. I really, really (really) wanted to random()-ly position dots around, but that would have taken a lot of empty individual elements (e.g., ) in the markup. Not my favorite. So, I generate the elements in PHP:.

I really, really wanted to random()-ize all the things, but inlining random coordinates on each was the way to go. Same deal with the inlined styles that set a fill, and sizing for each circle in the texture, and variables that set a --delay and --dur on the subtle animation that twinkles them in and out.

I’ll have to look at generating the SVG using or whatever later since that pattern repeats in the footer, too.

That’s carried through to the 404 page as well:.

If your browser supports border-shape and random() (only Chrome, I think), then the homepage gives you a blobby-blob shape behind the grid of author avatars. Hover it and it gets, you know, even blobbier.

It takes an existing pattern I’m calling .gradient-card:.

…and sets a gradient on the component’s :before pseudo:.

That sits underneath the :after pseudo that’s translucent, allowing the :before‘s gradient to show through a smidge:.

Industry observers note that the differing border-radius values allow :before to bleed outside, giving the impression of a border around the entire deal. That’s the basic shape. The border-shape is where things get blobby:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to shape()s. I grabbed the first one from Temani Afif’s blob generator:.

According to recent reports, it’s called “static” because that’s the default state. Hover or focus on the component and it swaps out those points out with a “hover” version of the shape:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to random() values:.

In a recent development, so, the hover state is different on each page load. And we animate between the two:.

In a recent development, I’m pretty stoked on this one. The Almanac has grown, evolved, and just plain gotten great the past few years. But the primary page for it… not so great. It was definitely overshadowed by work on the pages inside it and never revisited beyond clickable cards to get to each feature subset.

Now the page is a real index of the CSS features that gets you where you need to go swiftly. Someone somewhere sometime did some sort of CSS periodic table. I forget where I’d seen that but the general idea sat with me and I thought I could pull it off. There’s nothing “tricky” about it but I love what the layout adds to the overall site.

This is another area that sorely needed love. Our guides have always been a vertical stack of items. The book effect was definitely cool, but I started believing that leaning on it as the main visual hook was holding things back from being more functional. With something like 27 guides, we’re talking about a lot of scrolling with no clear idea of what you’re going to see as you go.

Again, nothing “tricky” but I like the overall usefulness of the new layout. There’s a featured guide, a widget of newly added and updated guides, and a categorized grid of everything below that.

The pages that show all of an author’s published articles got a little spruce-up, too.

In a recent development, it’s a little change, really. The right sidebar was moved to the left and the author image and bio moved in, allowing the articles to creep up to the top. I hope to do more here since the small layout tweak opens up more opportunities.

Also need to do the larger Authors index, but another time.

In a recent development, this one’s just for those of us working in the WordPress editor. I don’t need a complete visual editor to get things done, but it is a nice affordance to have some of the front-end styles sneak into the editing UI for a better idea of what you’re working with.

It has been revealed that using Lighthouse to measure things like performance, accessibility, and best practices is woefully fraught with caveats, but there’s no reason to chuck it completely. I find them more fun than fact and I don’t mind the recommendations for improving things.

So, after a few runs and tweaks, here’s how things shook out theme-to-theme.

According to recent reports, I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. I’m happier with the boosts to accessibility and best practices. SEO? Meh. Don’t really care unless it’s hurting more important things like accessibility.

Again, very happy. There’s little I can do with time to first byte but everything else seems to clock in at least marginally better. The total page weight is a clear win and that’s probably what I care most about here.

Oh gosh, there’s a lot more but they’re mostly minor things that don’t bubble up to the front end. Sort of the same way browser changelogs have some generic line of “bug squashing” or whatever. In this case, it’s things like better post queries and breadcrumbs and function management and naming and… you get it.

There’s definitely so much more to do. And plenty of things I’m sure I missed or broke along the way. That’s just life and those will have to come in another iterative release less worthy of a version bump. You can let me know what I muffed up in the comments.

I hope you at least like where this is going!

#138442. Latest Update: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports metadata pre-filtering for higher recall on filtered searches

📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)

Latest Update: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports metadata pre-filtering for higher recall on filtered searches

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search.
  • Most applications never search a whole index.
  • Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search. You can filter on attributes such as tenant, category, status, or time, and pre-filtering adds prefix matching with $startsWith for paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. Each vector carries up to 2 KB of filterable metadata, and a single query supports up to 100 filter constraints. There is no additional cost, no re-ingestion, and no change to your queries.

Most applications never search a whole index. They search the part of it that belongs to a particular user, account, or category, and they express that scope as a metadata filter. Semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic applications all need the same thing from a filtered query: a similarity search that covers the vectors matching the filter, and returns the closest of them. With pre-filtering, a filtered query returns more of the relevant matches your index contains, giving you higher recall on filtered searches.

Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:.

How pre-filtering works Each vector in an S3 Vectors index can carry application-defined metadata, and a query can filter on those fields.

Every vector index has an index mode. On an index whose index mode is ENHANCED, S3 Vectors resolves your filter first, then searches only the vectors that match. On an index whose index mode is CLASSIC, S3 Vectors performs the vector search and filter evaluation in tandem, validating each candidate vector against your filter as it searches. Existing indexes use CLASSIC until you update them.

Consider a support knowledge base of 8 million tickets, where an agent searches one customer’s history for a recurring error. If that customer accounts for 400 of those tickets, resolving customer_id first means the similarity search runs across all 400 of them, so the agent sees that customer’s prior occurrences. Before the index was updated, the same query drew its candidates from the full 8 million, and the result set contained fewer of that customer’s matching tickets.

On highly selective filters, pre-filtering returns up to 5x more of the matching vectors than the same query returned before on CLASSIC indexes.

Getting started Before you start, make sure your IAM policy grants permissions for the upcoming actions.

The dimension must match the output size of your embedding model, and distance-metric should match how that model was trained (cosine is common for text embeddings). Second, write vectors with the PutVectors API, attaching up to 2 KB of filterable metadata to each vector:.

Each vector carries the attributes your application filters on. In this example, tenant_id scopes results to a single customer, category narrows by document type, created_date records when the document was created, and active is a boolean flag. By default every metadata field is filterable, so you can query on any of them without declaring a schema up front.

Sources indicate that third, run a filtered similarity query with the QueryVectors API. The filter uses a compact JSON syntax where a bare key-value pair is an equality match, and operators such as $and, $or, and $gt combine or refine conditions. Pass --return-metadata so the query returns each vector’s metadata:.

The expected result is a single vector, doc-001, the only one matching all three filter conditions (tenant_id, category, and active):.

S3 Vectors first narrows the search space to vectors matching all three filter conditions, then returns the 50 most similar vectors from that subset. Because the filter is applied before the search, those results are drawn from across all the vectors that match it.

Recent findings suggest that prefix matching with $startsWith Pre-filtering adds a prefix match operator for filtering on paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. A document store that encodes case and folder structure into a document ID can scope a search to a subtree in one condition:.

$startsWith joins the existing operators: equality, numeric range, set membership, existence checks, and boolean logic with $and and $or.

Turning on pre-filtering for existing indexes Call UpdateIndexMode on an existing index to turn on pre-filtering:.

It has been revealed that pre-filtering takes effect in place. Your existing vectors are not re-ingested, your queries do not change, and the new filter operators are available immediately.

It has been revealed that here is the difference on the same index and the same query. Before the update, a query scoped to one tenant returns two of the ten results requested:.

After the upgrade, the same query returns a full result set drawn from across that tenant’s documents:.

Rolling out across your indexes Once you have validated pre-filtering on an index, set the default index mode on the vector bucket so that upcoming indexes use ENHANCED without a follow-up call:.

To bring the rest of your existing indexes across, list them and check the index mode on each one, then call UpdateIndexMode on the ones still using CLASSIC:.

In a recent development, now available Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. You pay standard S3 Vectors pricing for storage, PUT requests, and queries. For full pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page. For regional availability, visit Amazon S3 Vectors Regions and quotas.

Industry observers note that whether you’re scoping a RAG application to one tenant, scoping an agent’s searches to one user’s documents, or narrowing a catalog search to a licensing window, pre-filtering lets you apply those filters without trading away recall. To learn more and get started, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation. Send feedback to AWS re:Post for S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shortened burn leaves probe in a 75-hour orbit, but ESA claims December separation remains on schedule.
  • A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9.
  • According to recent reports, ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shortened burn leaves probe in a 75-hour orbit, but ESA claims December separation remains on schedule.

A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9.

According to recent reports, ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit. The burn began at 1824 UTC, when BepiColombo was approximately 635 km above the planet's surface. It was supposed to last for 37 minutes but shut down early.

The shutdown, caused by a software problem involving attitude guidance and thruster control, left the spacecraft in safe mode, a protective state in which all non-essential activities cease.

Ignacio Tanco, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Operations Director, said: "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened.".

The burn achieved around 77 percent of the planned velocity change, securing an orbit around Mercury but leaving BepiColombo taking 75 hours to circle the planet instead of the intended 58.

The good news is that multiple burns were always going to be needed to adjust the orbit ahead of Mio separation and MPO reaching its science orbit. "The remaining MOI [Mercury Orbit Insertion] sequence has already been adapted to the new trajectory, with no additional burns required," ESA stated.

"After each burn, the Flight Dynamics team determines the achieved orbit to then design the next manoeuvre," noted Frank Budnik, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Dynamics Manager.

It has been revealed that "So, the sequence is not only more propellant-efficient, it also allows Flight Dynamics to adapt each subsequent burn to the spacecraft's actual trajectory. It's a dynamic sequence! Each upcoming manoeuvre is based on the previous ones.".

Teams at ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) and Airbus continue to investigate the underlying software fault.

ESA has not remarked whether the revised burn sequence will affect propellant reserves available for a possible mission extension.

It has been revealed that the separation of Mio and MPO is planned for December 9, and more burns will be needed to guide MPO to its final orbit by March 2027, with science operations starting in April 2027. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily.

In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”.

According to recent reports, aware of an older source? Please comment!

The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY, “don’t repeat yourself”, in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition.

So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule:.

Industry observers note that the outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how significant file size savings are.

In a recent development, if you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today?

When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work.

To save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition.

Skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works). This, then, gives us some data:.

Sources indicate that for the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings.

Recent findings suggest that I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance.

Important note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality—they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. Also note that this leaves out changes after compression—this was not part of the experiment but would be fair to test, too.

For the question whether UDJO still works today, this should be a yes. It works as well as to even come with file size savings.

Maybe you’re curious, too, about what the situation looks like in our field, among web developers. Let’s take some samples on this, too.

It would be valuable to expand this analysis to take more samples and investigate the differences across samples, but there may be something to web professionals using shorter selectors so as to be able to benefit more from UDJO.

As mentioned at the beginning, UDJO’s effectiveness generally depends on the kind of repetition as well as on the length of selectors.

This can be managed, however: While tools like CSS Dedup make no difference between declaration use cases (and are therefore blunt), it is possible to configure them so as to reap the performance benefits.

As the data taken for this article suggest, file size savings may be achieved in most cases. Considering that this is based on safe changes, this means a low-cost performance optimization vector — especially when applied to minified output. It’s still a good idea to couch that against the use of further compression (e.g. gzip/Brotli), but at face value, deduplication demonstrates how it can reduce the size of CSS.

For anyone generally interested in CSS optimization, maintainability, and performance, UDJO should probably be part of the overall approach to CSS. But since the technique has been niche and since tooling is new, I invite you to review, test, and explore this vector. It seems hard to argue that we have reached the ceiling of how far we can take CSS optimization.

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and revealed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs.
  • It has been revealed that equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance.
  • Recent findings suggest that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and revealed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

It has been revealed that equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:.

Recent findings suggest that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

It has been revealed that not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:.

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Industry observers note that already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

It has been revealed that what puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

In a recent development, "Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:.

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

No model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

It has been revealed that we evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Industry observers note that both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

Industry observers note that the number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:.

Sources indicate that reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

In a recent development, A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:.

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

In a recent development, memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

Sources indicate that the real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

The lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:.

It has been revealed that A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

It has been revealed that memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Industry observers note that isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):.

TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Sources indicate that really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification. You can create V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables to take advantage of V3 features like deletion vectors, row lineage, and new data types such as variant, nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry, and geography.

Recent findings suggest that apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data in open Parquet files in data lakes on object storage like Amazon S3. Amazon S3 Tables offer storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with fully managed features like automatic compaction, maintenance, replication, and Intelligent-Tiering.

According to recent reports, teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows. A compliance request to delete 50,000 user records from a 2-billion-row table leaves behind positional delete files that slow queries until compaction runs. Semi-structured events land as JSON strings that every query has to parse. Geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision timestamps get encoded as strings or integers. Each workaround adds storage cost, query latency, and pipeline code. With V3, Iceberg solves these challenges by offering native support for semi-structured and geospatial data, faster row-level operations, and built-in row lineage for data governance.

Starting today, Amazon S3 Tables support all V3 data types, including variant, nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography, and unknown, along with deletion vectors and row lineage. You can create latest V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables in place, and S3 Tables continue to run compaction and maintenance for you.

Recent findings suggest that apache Iceberg V3 V3 is the latest version of the Iceberg specification. Among its many improvements, V3 introduces capabilities that address the most common pain points in V2. This includes:.

Deletion vectors replace V2’s positional delete files with a compact binary format. That 50,000-row compliance delete now writes a single deletion vector file instead of thousands of small deletes, significantly reducing compaction time and delete file overhead.

Row lineage adds _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number to each record automatically. Your downstream pipelines can query these fields to find changed rows without scanning the full table.

Upcoming data types let you store semi-structured, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision data natively instead of encoding it as strings or integers:.

In a recent development, variant data type stores semi-structured data in columnar format. During writes, the engine shreds variant data into hidden columns and collects statistics. At query time, those statistics enable file pruning that significantly reduces I/O compared to parsing JSON strings.

The following sections walk through how to use these V3 capabilities in practice, with examples that show how to create tables, work with the upcoming data types, and manage data at scale.

In a recent development, getting started A retail analytics team tracks user behavior across web and mobile apps. Each event has a different structure: page views include URLs and duration, purchases include items and amounts, and searches include query terms and result counts. With V3’s variant type, you store all event shapes in one table without predefined schemas:.

Insert events with different payload shapes without worrying about schema evolution:.

In a recent development, now query the variant column directly, without PARSE_JSON at read time. With Amazon EMR Spark, use variant_get:.

To enable deletion vectors for write operations, configure merge-on-read mode:.

Now when you run a compliance delete, V3 writes a small deletion vector instead of rewriting data files:.

S3 Tables compaction handles these deletion vector files automatically on the next maintenance cycle.

Upgrading from V2 AWS provides backwards compatibility for both versions to minimize disruption during migration to V3. Existing V2 readers continue to work on upgraded tables until you’re ready to fully adopt V3 features. For more details, see the S3 Tables Iceberg V3 documentation. Upgrade an existing table atomically without rewriting data:.

According to recent reports, on the next compaction cycle, S3 Tables remove old V2 delete files. Fresh modifications use deletion vectors automatically. Row lineage fields initialize on the first data modification after the upgrade.

This is a one-way operation. The Apache Iceberg specification does not support downgrading from V3 to V2. Verify that all engines accessing the table support V3 before upgrading.

Using row lineage for incremental pipelines After your table has V3 data, use row lineage to build efficient incremental pipelines:.

This returns only rows modified after sequence number 42. Your downstream jobs can checkpoint this value and process only latest changes on each run, instead of scanning the full table.

Sources indicate that compatibility across AWS analytics services AWS offers the broadest native Apache Iceberg support of any major cloud provider, with Iceberg-compatible services at every layer of the data stack: ingestion, storage, catalog, and analytics. You can store and automatically optimize V3 tables in Amazon S3 Tables, write data with Amazon EMR Spark, integrate and manage data with AWS Glue, and run analytics with Amazon Redshift. To learn more about AWS analytics support for V3, see the Apache Iceberg on AWS prescriptive guidance.

Both S3 Tables and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) API, enabling interoperability across engines regardless of the catalog endpoint.

Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

Industry observers note that the Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

Sources indicate that in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

According to recent reports, within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

In a recent development, streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • In a recent development, when CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.
  • Twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

In a recent development, when CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

Twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

Frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the company I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

According to recent reports, before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the company I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

Recent findings suggest that these questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional company I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

It has been revealed that wheelman isn’t an ordinary company, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

That doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the tech giant, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

Sources indicate that let’s imagine I’m designing a new landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Sources indicate that before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

Industry observers note that only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

Industry observers note that I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

According to recent reports, wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

According to recent reports, using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

The modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

The result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

It has been revealed that one thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

Wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

In a recent development, A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

In a recent development, the point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same tech giant.

Twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

Wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

And this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

That’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.

It has been revealed that pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are open! Everyone who pre-orders will also receive the Hardboiled Client Interview Guide for free — a practical companion to help designers ask better questions and discover what makes a organization distinctive.

The book will be published on November 20, priced at $14.99 for the DRM-free EPUB and PDF editions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • EU Academy names and email addresses exposed, with users warned via website notice rather than contacted directly.
  • The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected customers directly.
  • Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EU Academy names and email addresses exposed, with users warned via website notice rather than contacted directly.

The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected customers directly.

Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm.

The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution.

Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday.

"There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier remarked.

The notice warns owners that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities.

In a recent development, the trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice notes the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred.

The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create latest accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points.

The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data.

The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected customers sufficient.

"I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority.".

The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing.

The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns.

More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers.

"As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he noted. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound.
  • Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:.

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.

It has been revealed that we follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

Industry observers note that we measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

In a recent development, for LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:.

Recent findings suggest that then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

Industry observers note that the block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:.

We can’t wait to see what you build.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

Sources indicate that the agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:.

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

In a recent development, create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

In a recent development, you can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

Sources indicate that when you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

Recent findings suggest that you can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

You can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

It has been revealed that choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to patch your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

Industry observers note that you can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

Join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support strategy.

CrowdStrike splashes $44B on Zscaler, customers brace for the bill
