💡 Key Takeaways
  • Servo 0.8.0 contains all of the changes we landed in October, spanning 588 commits (a new record)!
  • Servo now renders subtitles and captions over elements (@TimvdLippe, #48809)!
  • Flutter web content no longer hangs now that we fixed a serious performance problem with typed arrays (@jdm, #48640).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus WebAudio nodes, image inputs, and more!

Servo 0.8.0 contains all of the changes we landed in October, spanning 588 commits (a new record)!

Servo now renders subtitles and captions over elements (@TimvdLippe, #48809)!

We’ve shipped latest web platform features:.

Flutter web content no longer hangs now that we fixed a serious performance problem with typed arrays (@jdm, #48640). Example.

According to recent reports, we’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub issues.

Sources indicate that with respect to accessibility in Servo, we report many more ARIA roles for DOM elements (@alice, @mrobinson, #48839). These can be inspected with the Get Computed Role WebDriver command (@lolaodelola, #47339). Accessibility integration can be turned on with the accessibility_enabled preference.

Sources indicate that webGL2 support received lots of attention this month, with fixes to getParameter(), drawBuffers(), readBuffers(), vertexAttribIPointer(), DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT, getUniformLocation(), vertexAttrib4x(), pixelStorei(), texStorage2D(), texStorage3D(), texImage3D(), getInternalformatParameter(), blitFramebuffer(), and texSubImage2D() (@mxmgorin, #48651, #48620, #48678, #48689, #48751, #48681, #48911, #48972, #48590, #49201, #49289, #48560, #48571). The feature remains gated behind the dom_webgl2_enabled preference.

Reading and writing mapped WebGPU buffers got a significant speed increase (@sagudev, @jdm, #48372). WebGPU can be enabled with the dom_webgpu_enabled preference.

JS script compilation can now occur off the main thread when the dom_script_asynch preference is enabled (@Gae24, #45687). Right now this only applies to non-module scripts.

Recent findings suggest that initial support for the backdrop-filter property has merged (@shubhamg13, #48829). This can be enabled with the layout_css_backdrop_filter_enabled preference.

Industry observers note that serviceWorkers now fire the statechange event when changing states during initialization (@gterzian, #48749). ServiceWorkerContainer can listen for message and messageerror events (@gterzian, #48680). Service Workers remain gated behind the dom_serviceworker_enabled preference.

The Geolocation API has been implemented (@webbeef, #48406). No platform-specific backends to provide the device geolocation data have merged yet, so it remains disabled behind the dom_geolocation_enabled preference.

DOM interfaces for MathML elements now exist, gated behind the mathml_core_enabled preference (@tannal, #48631). There is no MathML-specific layout implemented yet.

Industry observers note that A new, native SVG implementation is in progress (@mu-mostafa98, @jdm, #48467). This work is still in the early stages, but is intended to replace Servo’s dependency on the resvg crate to better integrate with page styling and animations.

IndexedDB cursors now support the update() and delete() methods (@kuntal-devrat, #48402). The feature can be enabled with the dom_indexeddb_enabled preference.

Industry observers note that support for LargestContentfulPaint performance timing improved, with image URLs (@shubhamg13, #48668), the loadTime value (@shubhamg13, #48676), ignoring non-paintable elements (@shubhamg13, #48856, #48898), video URLs (@shubhamg13, #48931), and following containing blocks (@shubhamg13, #48551). This work is behind the largest_contentful_paint_enabled preference.

According to recent reports, we added support for a new performance timing metric: ContainerTiming (@jasonwilliams, #46966). This can be enabled with the container_timing_enabled preference.

Recent findings suggest that our support for adoptedStylesheets improved along with a newly introduced implementation of the ObservableArray specification concept (@jerensl, @arihant2math, #48506). This is currently hidden behind the dom_adoptedstylesheet_enabled preference.

In a recent development, the Android Compose migration is complete, and embedders now only need to interact with the Servo library component (@veyndan, #48592, #48601, #48595, #48574, #48609, #48778, #48780, #49266). Embedders no longer need to trigger the soft keyboard display; this is controlled by a parameter to the Servo component (@veyndan, #48757).

There’s a new API method to report the network status of the embedder: NetworkManager::set_online_state (@xbwwj, #47568). This data is exposed via the onLine property of the Navigator interface in web content.

In a recent development, embedders can now disable all support for developer tools, which can reduce the size of the final binary (@janeoa, #47255). This is controlled by the devtools feature and enabled by default; it is also part of the new default_tooling feature.

It has been revealed that consumers of the C API can set preferences that accept f64 and f64 array parameters (@fran6co, #49325), as well as the HiDPI scale factor for each WebView (@fran6co, #49327). WebViews can also be resized via the C API (@fran6co, #49326).

The layout_grid_enabled preference has been removed, since CSS Grid now defaults to enabled (@Loirooriol, #48718). Several preferences were renamed (@nicoburns, #48915):.

Double and triple clicking on selected text will extend the selection to the current word and line, respectively (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #48767).

Clicking a link with the middle mouse button now opens up the link in a fresh WebView (@SteveSharonSam, @mrobinson, #46000).

Range inputs can be dragged with the mouse (@webbeef, #48342).

Command+delete on macOS will delete the preceding line in a text control (@dzfrias, #48781).

The developer tools continue to improve:.

We improved exception error messages related to the XMLHttpRequest, History, Range, Selection, Element, CharacterData, and DOMTokenList interfaces, and namespaces and attributes (@gabrielecabrini, #49146, #49145, #48786, #49102).

Media elements that start playing outside of a document will no longer be garbage collected until playback finishes (@sabbCodes, @jdm, #49367, #48979).

Pinch zoom operations no longer have to rebuild a full display list, making zooming complex pages much smoother (@stevennovaryo, @mrobinson, #43561).

In a recent development, we improved performance in many small and focused ways by doing less work during restyling and layout (@SimonSapin, @webbeef, @nicoburns, @mrobinson, #49137, #49100, #48485, #48968), reducing GC interactions (@mrobinson, @jschwe, #48984, #49140, #49195, #49425), and delaying work on disconnected trees (@SimonSapin, #49098). We also fixed instances of quadratic layout with deep nesting (@nicoburns, #49148) and missing caching (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #49164, #49073).

We fixed some intermittent GC panics when notifying ResizeObservers (@mrobinson, #49189), introspecting keyframes (@MohamedAli00949, #48546), setting timers (@jdm, #48548), using writable streams (@jdm, #48656), and scrolling iframes after removing them (@mrobinson, #49230).

We also fixed numerous other panics and crashes in scrollable and incremental layout (@mrobinson, #49230, #49283), moving nodes around (@mrobinson, #49226), using WebGPU from opaque origins (@gabrielecabrini, #49207), stringifying some WebIDL types (@mrobinson, #49374), using readable streams (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #49311), clicking disabled file controls (@mrobinson, #49379), rendering giant SVGs (@sabbCodes, #49264), unminifying JS (@jdm, #48567), measuring text (@mxmgorin, #48621), rendering text tracks (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48827), preparing dialogs (@lukewarlow, #49431), and running delayed tasks in destroyed documents (@mrobinson, @jdm, #49399, #48714).

In a recent development, many small-to-medium improvements to reduce allocations were merged (@yezhizhen, @Narfinger, @Taym95, @mrobinson, @Loirooriol, @CynthiaOketch, @sabbCodes, @mxmgorin, #48549, #48558, #48568, #48598, #48615, #48565, #48646, #48654, #48569, #48562, #48588, #48650, #48702, #48675, #48589, #48720, #48721, #47720, #48745, #48703, #48750, #48770, #48789, #48754, #48828, #48838, #48836, #48841, #48843, #48867, #48882, #48842, #48881, #48840, #48899, #48924, #48904, #48949, #48953, #48980, #49028, #48885, #49035, #49038, #49084, #49131, #49125, #48951, #49154, #49160, #49198, #49202, #49194, #49219, #49258, #49275, #49295, #49298, #49300, #49320, #49323, #49313, #49373, #49380, #48969, #48991). We also reduced memory usage by shrinking some types (@Narfinger, @webbeef, #48954, #48082, #48906).

Memory leaks received a lot of attention this month, covering everything from network requests, to JS modules, to timer tasks, and more (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, @jschwe, #48952, #48957, #49032, #49049, #49092, #49134, #49139, #49132, #48747, #48752).

We continue to work towards preventing certain sources of memory leaks with static analysis and the Rust type system (@Gae24, @Narfinger, @jdm, #48147, #48360, #48832, #48887, #48913, #48903, #48965, #48905, #48834, #48855, #49083, #49082, #49081, #49096, #49135, #49130).

We fixed bugs related to the CORS preflight cache (@sabbCodes, #49055, #49252), fetch metadata (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48793), HTTP cache revalidation (@mrobinson, @jdm, #48927), image load timing (@mrobinson, @TimvdLippe, #48902, #48790, #48599), touch events (@yezhizhen, #48671, #48699, #48701), cloning and moving input elements (@skyz1, @mrobinson, #48845, #48069), the :indeterminate pseudoclass (@skyz1, #48070), stylesheet introspection (@mrobinson, #48935), mutating ranges (@gabrielecabrini, #49072), blob URLs (@rogerkorantenng, #49074, #48989, #49206), form controls (@mrobinson, @lukewarlow, @jdm, #49163, #49225, #48513), the mapping property of Gamepad (@msub2, #49381), beforeinput events (@dzfrias, #48825), image dimensions (@TimvdLippe, #49085), table appearance attributes (@Loirooriol, #49120, #49108, #49156, #49150), IME events (@dzfrias, #48690), reconnecting IntersectionObserver (@shubhamg13, #48581), and root elements (@TimvdLippe, #48514).

We also addressed layout problems related to soft wrap line breaks (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48564), grid and flex layouts with indefinite dimensions (@RichardTjokroutomo, @rayguo17, @nicoburns, #48670, #48644, #49232), hanging whitespace (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48591, #48753), preserve-3d (@mrobinson, #47933), inline block splits (@Loirooriol, #46445), video controls (@rayguo17, #44956), display: contents (@Loirooriol, #48784, #48785), justify-contents (@yezhizhen, #48746, #48988), absolute positioning (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48846), (@Loirooriol, #49143), text-transform: capitalize (@jschwe, #48901), incremental table layout (@Loirooriol, #49176), width: stretch (@Loirooriol, #49239, #49237), backface visibility (@mrobinson, #49196), flex gaps (@yezhizhen, #49335), perspective (@mrobinson, #49174), quirks mode (@Loirooriol, #48942, #39869, #48978, #49211), SVG viewboxes (@leowatts, #48556), ISO-8859-8 documents (@TTyChud, #48444), and table borders (@adoublebarrel, @mrobinson, #47684).

A special thanks to the following people for landing their first patch in Servo:.

Recent findings suggest that interested in helping build a web browser? Take a look at our curated list of issues that are good for new contributors!

It has been revealed that thanks again for your generous support! We are now receiving 8057 USD/month (-2% from September) in recurring donations. This helps us cover the cost of our speedy CI and benchmarking servers, one of our latest Outreachy interns, and funding maintainer work that helps more people contribute to Servo, as well as feature development.

Servo is also on thanks.dev, and already 37 GitHub consumers (+0 from September) that depend on Servo are sponsoring us there. If you use Servo libraries like url, html5ever, selectors, or cssparser, signing up for thanks.dev could be a good way for you (or your employer) to give back to the community.

According to recent reports, we now have sponsorship tiers that allow you or your organisation to donate to the Servo project with public acknowlegement of your support. If you’re interested in this kind of sponsorship, please contact us at [email protected].

Use of donations is decided transparently via the Technical Steering Committee’s public funding request process, and active proposals are tracked in servo/project#187. For more details, head to our Sponsorship page.

GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • Sources indicate that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

Sources indicate that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

Sources indicate that that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

According to recent reports, we removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Sources indicate that reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in consumers. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind initiative. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to patch, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

According to recent reports, actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

Sources indicate that A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

In a recent development, the importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One upcoming machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, newly introduced commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Sources indicate that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Industry observers note that some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

Sources indicate that we took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Industry observers note that audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Problems, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Newly introduced requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

It has been revealed that the pool was already running near capacity when some enhancement requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ICO reprimand follows failings that risked wrongful detention, with a temporary correction process taking more than a year to arrive.
  • The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information.
  • The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ICO reprimand follows failings that risked wrongful detention, with a temporary correction process taking more than a year to arrive.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information.

The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm.

The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month.

Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border.

Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records.

Recent findings suggest that platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time.

Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction.

One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was introduced on October 2.

The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios.

Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff mentioned they didn't know how to request data corrections.

During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data.

The Home Office later stated that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have.

But the Home Office also stated that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach.

The ICO remarked in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the fresh, accurate information that should be used to replace it.

The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out noted personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome.".

It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy complications.

The new method went live on October 25, 2025.

By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed.

The ICO mentioned it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed.

The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks.

It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however.

"The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated.

According to recent reports, A Home Office spokesperson told us: "We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates."Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security.".

Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected.

In a recent development, "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay.".

Recent findings suggest that the ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice.

In a recent development, fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants, and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information, including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • Industry observers note that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Industry observers note that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

In a recent development, holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

In a recent development, automationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. Sources indicate that trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

Sources indicate that no one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

Industry observers note that our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Sources indicate that opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

In a recent development, both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Update: We will be providing a technical blog with details in the coming weeks once our full investigation is complete.
  • According to recent reports, on November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
  • The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update: We will be providing a technical blog with details in the coming weeks once our full investigation is complete.

According to recent reports, on November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:.

Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times.

Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security).

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account).

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers).

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of consumers in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.

Your vaults and the items in them.

The keys that protect your vaults.

1Password does not store your account password or secret key.

1Password apps and browser extensions.

Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.

Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added fresh detections for this kind of attack.

Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.

According to recent reports, 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a upcoming device or browser.

Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.

If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.

In a recent development, you trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.

Industry observers note that we are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • In a recent development, our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this strategy includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

In a recent development, our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this strategy includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern highlights up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

Sources indicate that A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

According to recent reports, provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Recent findings suggest that those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

Sources indicate that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

According to recent reports, the most direct result is this: experts noted 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

According to recent reports, in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an crucial area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This highlights it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Industry observers note that blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Sources indicate that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

According to recent reports, source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

According to recent reports, practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval states "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Industry observers note that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

In a recent development, I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Recent findings suggest that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

In a recent development, hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.
  • Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall.
  • It has been revealed that if anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.

SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.

It has been revealed that if anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

Sources indicate that we also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with significant industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.

The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that presently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

According to recent reports, what's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for newly introduced datacenter builds.

Sources indicate that the power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power  – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

In a recent development, water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a significant deal.

The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a latest build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.

Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the fresh set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

According to recent reports, at SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

It has been revealed that any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

In a recent development, my instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

In a recent development, there's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing indicates 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.

We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.

In a recent development, much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®.

Industry News: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve.
  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. Upcoming research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

The report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

Recent findings suggest that the research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

Recent findings suggest that AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates latest risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

Industry observers note that virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

The survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain important, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

According to recent reports, for platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly key infrastructure considerations.

The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.
