📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure).

Laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.

Recent findings suggest that laura Savino a software engineer at Adobe Photoshop. She brings her background in education and humanities to technical topics, creating talks that spark ongoing conversations.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Laura Savino: Several friends and colleagues have come to me to tell me recently that they are pregnant with their first child, and have taken comfort from a really odd bit of perspective that I've given them, because I have two lovely kids, two very much wanted and uneventful pregnancies. I hated being pregnant. Every so often, I look around a crowd of people, and I'm like, everyone here is the result of a pregnancy, and it creeps me out. It's beautiful. It's a miracle of life. It is also not my jam. The thing that made me willing to do it at all and that gave me great comfort along the way was actually the myth of the frog. This frog is swimming around in water that starts at a comfortable temperature, but is slowly heated through to a boil, and if you do it gradually enough, the frog won't really notice that its environment is no longer like anything it's ever experienced before, and the frog is eventually cooked.

Sources indicate that this odd myth gave me a lifeline of hope, because if that frog can adapt to extreme, unprecedented conditions, so can I. Because the difficult parts usually come on gradually, day by day. If having a child started with the eighth-month pregnancy discomfort, very few of us would do it. It would be banned as inhumane torture if we could instantly make people eight months pregnant.

Some of you are like, "It's 9:00 in the morning. We're at a software conference. Can we please not talk about spontaneous advanced gestation? It is a repulsive idea." When we see a person eight months pregnant who got there gradually, the way we all luckily do, we just think, how nice. It's not repulsive at all, it's beautiful. It's usually obvious that they're just handling it like champions. It turns out the frog thing is thoroughly debunked. At a certain point, ectotherms change locations to keep themselves safe. The myth works to reassure me and my pregnant friends because of the way I frame it. It's not that the thing gets worse and worse slowly, and you don't notice and eventually are cooked. It's that you yourself change. You adapt. Yes, your context becomes more and more difficult, but if you're committed to sticking it out, you flex some increasingly creative coping strategies and skills, you become able to handle it. You worry about eighth month after you've figured out the seventh month and the sixth month, you'll be fine.

In a recent development, let's tangent from there. I have these two amazing kids, one is 8. We've had Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse on repeat in our house this past month. There's this one scene that captures me. A newly bitten Spider-Man is trying to learn to thwip, that's the technical term, and he's doing it while being chased by an evil giant robo-scientist through the trees, so Spider-Man is like dodging trees, and he yells, "Whoa, whoa, I can't do this yet." His trainer quips, "Everyone knows that the best way to learn is under intense, life-threatening pressure." Another anecdote. My friend TJ. TJ is an all-around delightful person, but their rarest trait and the highest compliment that I can reach for is that they are a functional programming language aficionado and are not an asshole about it. These days we're all a little or a lot more on board with the functional aspects of Rust and Kotlin and Swift, and strongly preferring pure functions is just mainstream now.

According to recent reports, side Effect punk is dead. Remember Haskell, the language? Remember when there was a whole functional programming dogma with true believers, with the hyper-conviction of the newly converted, and there were memes about monads. If your brain could follow certain logical compressions, you were with it. You were good. You were likely to survive, and everybody else was getting left in the imperative rubble. When I learned TJ appreciated Haskell, I was like, but you're so chill about it. They were like, it's a really interesting tool. This was the first time that I'd met a functional programming enthusiast that I could relate to.

In a recent development, I am Laura Savino. I'm a developer on Photoshop, somewhat on the iOS UI, but also on the C++ library that supports real Photoshop PSD file editing on your phone. Before I became a software engineer, I thought I was going to be a language teacher. I was for a minute. I took master's-level courses in things like how to teach American English pronunciation, how to design a test that tests what you want it to evaluate, which is hard. I taught English in France and French in Seattle, and English again at that time in South Korea, and eventually learned to code. Fast-forward several years, and here I am on the QCon London stage. Today's talk, I hope, will start to shift your identity from someone who's good at doing a specific thing to someone who's good at learning near anything. I'm taking it as an anthology of vignettes with research for structural support. In rough order of appearance, so you have a sense of time passing. There will be cabinet-making, teen vampires, December-born horses, a Zen priest, football kits, awkward dance floors, and a puppy. I will provide a slide with references at the end, so you can settle in.

I started with three stories, one about a frog, one about Spider-Man, and one about these monad pushers, and this is not exactly an un-telegraphed reveal that these stories map shockingly neatly onto the onslaught of AI. The first one, the frog metaphor that comforted me so much in my pregnancy, part of what makes the AI transition so disorienting is that we're being asked, many of us, to take it on. Like, now, now, now, the water is plasma, and you frogs will get in there, and you will like it. If you're not already orchestrating, you're so far behind, you might as well take up goat herding, because the goats are more your speed. For Spider-Man, a significant reason the AI transition is so daunting is that many people's livelihoods are directly tied to how well we adapt. It's fine. The robot arm's chasing us, they're motivating. We all just ducked in here for a minute to throw them off our trails.

Sources indicate that lastly, about my chill friend, it's tough out there because of all the zealots. I think most of them are not actually assholes. I genuinely believe they're mostly just excited, and they cannot imagine a reasonable person in possession of all the facts who's not exactly as excited as they are. They respond by either assuming you're an unreasonable person or giving you more facts, and I'm not sure which is worse. The ultimate well-meaning zealot is the Chris Traeger character on Parks and Rec played by Rob Lowe. This character is intense, precise, and painfully optimistic. There's this one scene where he says he's logged 65,000 miles running in his lifetime, and his goal is to run to the moon. Some AI enthusiasts are giving a little Chris Traeger running to the moon. We recognize they're telling us about something healthy and good, and they may even have our best interests at heart, but no part of me wishes I had my running shoes on so I could join him to the moon. How do we bring people with us?

I experienced a massive at-the-time transition in Cocoa, in the Apple development community that did this well. See, it was possible for a long time to go into Apple development with a great deal of hubris. You were an Apple developer. You knew all the tricks and tips. You'd hand-molded a lock and knit release cycles. Back of the cabinet here means, sure, no one's going to see this part of the code, but we're still going to make it just so because we take pride in our work. For a minute there, you could be confident that your deep UI kit and Objective-C knowledge meant that big companies would pay you and a team of three or four devs and a crack designer, absolute truckloads of cash to write them an app because everyone needed apps and no one knew how to write them except us. It was a really good time to be an Apple developer.

Then Apple dropped Swift, brand new language. You're welcome, everyone. Soon all our new APIs will be in this brand-new language that you have to use. We were willing to give up our semicolons. No one likes those, but they ripped away our square brackets too. This was one of those watershed community moments. One perspective I really liked at the time was, we're knocked back to being beginners again, and we like it. We're on even footing. We're learning together. Isn't this exciting? The change electrified us in good and bad ways. On the good side, I distinctly remember watching people who'd shipped indie software on CDs, people who were intimately familiar with why NSString is prefixed that way because they used to code in NEXTSTEP. These developers dived headfirst into the new language. I was sitting around with The Omni Group folks, like OmniFocus, OmniGraffle, these are Apple ecosystem legends, with our laptops out in the hotel lobbies of San Francisco, just trying to figure out, what can I do with this new language? On the less good side.

Swift was announced in June, and on my production app, we had an intern who waited several weeks till late July, before Xcode, our IDE was even out of beta, the intern added Swift to the project just for fun. The tool chain support was abysmal. I couldn't exactly embrace the beginner's mind when I was trying to ship a feature and couldn't even type because my IDE kept lagging out with this message. It was frustrating and not at all production ready because the tool chain was literally in beta. On the whole, with the benefit of rose-colored nostalgia, it was good. Most super senior principal developers, these pinnacles of technical excellence, were having to relearn how to get the eighth element out of a string, like just rookie stuff. The behaviors that got rewarded were the ones where people learned in public. The people who learned the most were the ones who asked the most questions, who'd notice when they didn't understand something and say, this is something I don't understand.

Sources indicate that how interesting? They'd post forum questions and ask each other how things worked. They would post early code samples where they did not look like geniuses who knew all the answers, but just enthusiastic rookies who wanted to learn. You know how much people love correcting people on the internet, so anyone who posted something inaccurate got told about it real quick. How do you be ok with that, though? How do you psychologically handle going from the expert hot commodity to a total noob and keep up decent spirits while you do it?

My friends, has anyone considered the old standby straight-up denial? I don't think any of us are in first-order denial about AI where we refuse to accept that it exists or is changing things, but for myself, I am absolutely deep in second-order denial where you acknowledge the basic facts of the thing, but you deny the implications of those facts. Sure, the technology is here, but I am not ready to face its implications. I usually try to add a lot of details when I'm giving a talk, but here, I am going to kindly draw a veil and let the camera discreetly pan away because you do not need me to share my particular doomsday flavors. Besides, it weakens the denial. Denial can also stem from a fear that you or those you love lack the skills or resources to handle the consequences of a change. That's real.

In a recent development, apparently, denial can have protective effects, though. This one study, "The role of denial in recovery from coronary heart disease," found that people who were in deep denial actually had better short-term outcomes than the ones who were actually facing reality. If you had deeper denial, you'd spend less time in intensive care and have fewer heart-related symptoms while you were in hospital. This rings true for me. Even if I've decided a thing is important to me, even when it's well-aligned with my values, if I face the full implications of how hard it's going to be, I will probably not do it. I might say, I don't have to exercise at the gym. I'm just going to put my shoes on and show up and we'll just see what happens. Denial can work to get us to start down a hard road and give us hope long enough to adapt to this ever-changing water.

Protective denial, it's incredibly common. We're also all going to die someday, but memento mori has somehow fallen out of fashion. If you want to sit in second-order denial with me for a little longer, that's ok. For a little longer, because the heart patients with serious denial had worse outcomes long-term. They didn't follow their medical advice, because why would they? They were fine. They got re-hospitalized more. Denial is not sustainable. If a little self-misdirection is what it takes to follow your values to stay in the room and not make a down payment on a yacht, go ahead, indulge. Let me suggest another indulgence, brain candy. When I was trying to improve my Spanish, I read the Twilight books, and I'm guessing most of you haven't read them or won't admit to having read them, because they're cloying vampire, werewolf, romance novels written for pre-teens. My Spanish became tan brillante como el pelo de Eduardo a la luz del sol, because brain candy, in the domain you're trying to learn, is just like the little carrot thrown down the path to convince the recalcitrant, what, I'm supposed to be good at this part of you, to at least look over and start to think about how to maybe head down this otherwise daunting path.

It has been revealed that sometimes you truly need to lower the stakes mentally just so you can push through. Get out of that intense, life-threatening pressure. Solve an actual problem that only you have. Make some tool, make some toy, make a flatulence app with your 8-year-old, something real, but where no one will evaluate you on the outcome because evaluation changes us. We don't learn so we can achieve the task we care about, we learn to pass the test assigned to us. This is bad even if you're an excellent test taker.

I took a break from my French major one summer to spend eight weeks in an intensive Japanese language study in northern Japan, where they promised to teach us the equivalent of two university semesters of Japanese. I was very good at French at that point. I had just breezed through a pair of graduate seminars and my placement test in the Japanese program put me in the very lowest level class. I'd only taken two basic Japanese classes by this point, but I just still felt like, "Hello, don't you know who I am? I'm good at languages. Why am I in the beginner's class with these people who can barely put a sentence together?" Granted, I couldn't say, do you know who I am, in Japanese, which is maybe a sign that their class placement was somewhat valid, but I had a demonstrated skill in a fundamentally different but still related area.

Industry observers note that some of us are feeling this way about computing right now. I'm good at computers. I am a senior professional programmer. I once learned Python in an afternoon. If this new computing skill is hard for me, either is something is wrong with the system or something is wrong with me. Don't you know who I am? For me in Japan, my identity was so caught up in being good at languages that I worked hard to avoid ever making a mistake, not just on coursework, but asking the bus driver for a transfer ticket. I wanted my Japanese to be perfect. I actually learned the most about learning that summer on a weekend excursion, just me and a classmate, where we stayed at a family-run Buddhist temple out in the countryside. I won't go into the expectation thrashing experience of preparing myself for a solemn weekend of meditation and instead watching sumo wrestling on TV with a priest and his family, but the larger foundation-shattering surprise was the way my classmate spoke to our Japanese hosts and that she would just say things.

She'd trip over words. She'd mess up her verb endings. My grammar wasn't great, but I could recognize a bunch of mistakes even if I couldn't correct them. I was so deep in this prove to everyone that I'm good at this mentality that if I didn't know how to say something properly, I'd keep quiet so I didn't embarrass myself. Amy, though, just talked. They're like laughing, conversing. The priest gets another beer. What stuck with me long after I forgot all the extra kanji I learned that summer, is that interacting imperfectly builds fluency. You get early feedback before unwanted behaviors are calcified. Find your version of a Zen retreat where you can just play with the tools with no expectations of evaluation. You'll develop facility and fluency that much faster.

Industry observers note that another way to fail when something's not a test. Many years ago, as I was just learning to code, like mapping out how to do red-black trees on a whiteboard level, I went out with some friends and some friends of friends to rent a karaoke room. One of these friends of friends turned out to be an engineering manager at Microsoft, which is a hazard of where I live in Seattle. I remember the fear and dread and shame that I felt when I was unable to successfully navigate the karaoke interface via any of the in-room remote controls. See, I saw this as my chance to prove my technical prowess and maybe get hired on at Microsoft. Why would the engineering manager consider my resume if I couldn't even modify the output settings of a retro karaoke system? I don't remember what any of us saying, but I do remember holding that remote in my hand and thinking that I was never going to get a job in tech.

It has been revealed that now we're all looking back at 15 years ago me and inwardly shouting, everybody knows these systems are hard. Just try, don't give up, it's fine. We have so much compassion. What is your tool today that you're like, I still don't have this thing working. What are they all going to think of me? I better hide it and fake it and just play it cool. If you have that mental block, lower the stakes, make a tool, make a toy, something unspeakably inane that is tailored to exactly your interests. It can lower the activation energy required to take that next step towards learning.

Another way I make daunting things feel more approachable is thinking of them as a practice round. Picture this, every Sunday morning, I'm at a former aircraft hangar that's been turned into an indoor kids' sports hell hole arena. There are five football fields, a dozen simultaneous kid classes, there's adult workout classes, there's birthday rooms, plus an enormous bouncy house situation. I promise you whatever you're picturing, there are more bouncy houses. There's screaming and there's tears and there's kids running and begging for snacks, and I'm paying to be here. I went to great effort to dig the 4-year-old's soccer uniform out of his dirty laundry hamper and convince him to leave the house and convince him to leave the car. My reward for that is sitting on an uncomfortable bench drinking truly some of the worst coffee in Seattle. I want to paint for you this picture of aggressively, brightly colored despair, because what you need to appreciate is that it was a significant deal for me to change perspectives.

Recent findings suggest that because I realize that if you see this not as a whole collection of circumstances designed to maximize my suffering, but hundreds of families who each separately fought through the chaos that is having a child on a chilly, damp weekend morning and got them to leave the house. If we could see in a little heads-up display what people overcame to get through that door, we would be walking around high-fiving and pouring each other pints. Nobody mentions all these hurdles. They just act like, yes, kids are wearing their kits here on time, relatively few boogers, as if they didn't execute a dozen fancy maneuvers to get there. If I don't tell someone that I struggled to get my kid there dressed, I won't hear their advice. Yes, my kid sleeps in her football kit. Sunday mornings have become my time to bask in the glory that not only have all of us made it through a gauntlet, but we've also successfully identified flaws in our own getting-out-of-the-house systems.

We're basically red teaming our own lives. How did you do at getting out of the house without yelling and tears? C-minus. How will you do at learning from what went wrong? Are you committed to bringing better snacks next time? The point isn't how well you executed the thing today, but how well you've internalized and applied the changes for next time. Put the snacks in the car right now, and today counts as a success.

Sources indicate that when I was deciding whether to take this job I had at Photoshop, I called up a friend for advice, because I had two offers for very different jobs, one that I was sure I would be good at, that they would be lucky to have me, and the other was a stretch. It was on Photoshop, where I'd have to brush up on modern C++ and L1 caches and deal with real legacy code. My friend noted that if I had the appetite to learn the newly introduced thing, the hard thing, that I should do it now. Because at some point, he said, you're like, I don't want to learn a whole new paradigm again. I've been there. I've done that. I'm good. This advice was perfect when I was choosing my destiny, and learning modern C++ was supposed to be my last massive career challenge. Now, very few of us have a choice about whether to invest a ton of energy in learning this new thing.

I have to somehow generate energy for learning or hit burnout real hard. I feel like maybe external energy building works for salespeople. Like I could just shout, are you ready? Let's get pumped. Everyone would be like, yes, let's go. We're engineers who got to where we are by taking skepticism to an art form. How many people have looked at some shiny upcoming tech, remarked, no, and then just watched it crumble off into the sunset? No amount of like, rah, rah, do it, is going to convince us in all of the do it, learn, go. It's like being told by a scowling Simon Cowell to do a heartfelt interpretive dance. You're not at your best. How do we, the hopeful skeptics who do believe in a better future, in spite of it all, how do we generate energy to learn? Let's actually start by not spiraling, perhaps, by not leaking happiness.

Industry observers note that one way I patch the leak is comparing current me to past me, because I'm obviously better than I was 10 years ago, aren't you? Think of you 10 years ago, and the glimmers of what you most value now that we're just starting to show. We were all goobers then compared to us now. Yet, we are all deeply discounting how much wiser we will be in the next 10 years, because we've got it figured out now. This is an actual studied phenomenon with a whole name, the end of history illusion. More specifically, we see the present as the moment where we have finally become the person we'll be for the rest of our lives.

Recent findings suggest that more published sources. Just this year, Dr. Maya Shankar published a really timely book called "The Other Side of Change." I feel like she gets us as software people today, because she was well on the path to becoming a professional violinist when she had a career-ending injury, at which point she went into the field of psychology. She eventually became the behavioral sciences advisor to the UN. She did all right. I am clinging to her perspectives like a lifeline. She adds to this end of history idea, not about years, but any large change, when we imagine what it will be like to navigate an unexpected change and its aftermath, we tend to assume that we'll be the same person from beginning to end. Research shows that we greatly underestimate how much we'll change in the future, even though we fully acknowledge that we've changed considerably in the past.

Am I just going to keep reading you quotes? Yes, I am. Because these are literally professional studiers of brains, and they remarked this better than I can. You can think of this as the audiobook interlude. "The unique stresses and demands of being thrust into a upcoming reality can uncover unexpected insights about ourselves and the world around us. These insights, coupled with the experience of the change itself, can transform us in extraordinary ways." I hear that, and I externally nod. Like, yes, maybe I'll grow on the other side of whatever this unprecedented time is. Also, a small part of me throws an absolute foot-stomping fit. I do not want to. I've barely got it together with the current state of things, and now you're coming at me with, think of all the personal growth you'll get. Like, no, I'm sorry. How many people are actively fantasizing about goat-herding careers right now?

There is some comfort in knowing that the person who will undergo the full experience will be different from the person we are in this very moment. We will become latest people on the other side of change in ways we are capable of shaping. I still don't want to. I don't. I remind myself to take a breath, or six, because, see, the frog is facing physical challenges and doesn't have biohacking tools there in its pot. Our challenges are all in our minds, for better or worse. As my favorite book series notes, my head is where 90-plus percent of my problems are. We believe in neuroplasticity. We can change and grow our minds from the inside out. I promise this is related, but did you know in the competitive equine sports world, all horses have the same official birthday? In the Northern Hemisphere, they all turn one year older on January 1st.

Recent findings suggest that that means that if your horse was born on New Year's Eve, for juvenile racing purposes, they'll be considered 2 years old when they turn 366 days. You can see how a 700-day-old 2-year-old race horse would have an advantage. Breeders often arrange for foals to be born as close to January 2nd as they can. Football in the States has the same effect, actually, where a statistically improbable number of professional footballers are born in the first quartile of the year. Few parents initiative their kids' births around the football season for some reason. There's something to be said for always being a little ahead of your peer group. You literally win more. If the kids on your football team look up to you because they're barely 6 while you're nearly 7, and coaches look to you to lead the team's comeback when they're behind 3-0, you develop leadership skills and confidence from a very early age.

Sources indicate that I am on the other side. I came to technology late, so I got used to seeking coding advice from literal teenagers from day one of my first professional programming job. Since then, every team I'm on, I've been in the middle quartile in terms of raw technical Leet code acumen. Before anyone starts DMing me about imposter syndrome and telling me to believe in myself, I'm going to stop you, because I'm on the Photoshop engineering team, and I'm solidly in the middle of the pack. It's like being in the bottom third of Man City players, like, I'm one of the worst world-class athletes. Like, it's fine. I'm no slouch. I just keep moving up to better and better leagues. Because I started out behind and have stayed in the middle, I've never developed an ego around being the fastest prototyper or the most effective algorithm tuner. I have learned how to learn.

It has been revealed that there's this famous study on which learning tasks people will take if given the option to improve their skills. One task is advertised as majorly effective, the other as so-so. It turns out the researchers could easily influence which participants chose which task. See, in the ineffective task, people could try and fail privately, and the highly effective one involved practicing in front of the group so everyone saw your mistakes. Clearly different paths with different risks and outcomes, and you all might have a sense of which group you would tend towards. How would a researcher influence you to pick one over the other? They gave people reading material about the malleability of the particular skill, debating in this case. One group read that debate is mostly an innate skill, the other that anyone can do it. It just takes training. It takes practice. The people who were in the inborn skill group, they did not participate in the activity that would help them improve, because then everybody would see that they lacked the skill.

The trainable skill group people were like, ok, let's go. Who cares if other people see that I can't do this yet? Showing people you're ignorant of something today can and should be super low stakes. It goes along with believing in neuroplasticity. This study is out of Carol Dweck's research about growth mindset, which had a whole Silicon Valley trend moment. I think it's not as trendy now, but the research is still solid. People who believe that their traits and abilities can significantly change are more likely to engage in behaviors that improve them. One problem that I ran into face first, like a very clean plate glass door one, is that when you start paying attention to whether you have a growth mindset and realize that without the researcher's priming that you would definitely be in the group that's like, better make sure no one finds out I'm a terrible debater.

It throws you extra, because you, by definition, don't really believe that you can change how fixed your mindset is. These research scientists, I have to believe them because they approach this problem with rigor and with science at Stanford. They say quite plainly that cherished traits can be developed. I want to be better at believing in change and in neuroplasticity, so I'm working on it.

According to recent reports, part of my identity has become someone who learns out loud, and I've modeled learning out loud in public. The first time a principal engineer on the Photoshop team wanted to show me how to use a new AI tool to bolt a tricky feature onto our existing architecture, I recorded our screen share session and posted it for the rest of the team because seeing a tool used in a real-world context is always more instructive than the demo-worthy vacuum. Especially because, like all my comrades who brought their kids to weekend morning soccer practices, we each come to AI and use AI in completely different ways. My favorite take on this is from Dr. Cat Hicks. She is a research psychologist studying software teams and gets riled up in a very data-driven way when people talk about things like measuring team effectiveness. She emphasizes that none of us are having the same experience.

According to recent reports, "When you have a highly adaptive, dialogical tool," which means the user is in dialogue with the tool, "where the user is shaping the context and wielding progressive disclosure to probe very different parts of its capabilities, different people will continue to get very different answers. Until we get real about the personalized, adaptive nature of this." People are each running their own individual experiments with newly introduced tools, and if we don't tell each other what our own tool uses look like, no one will know that you can put your kid to bed already wearing their football kit. This is not the time to experiment alone until your output seems to resemble other people's. Plus, even if I just complain about a tool, I usually get some really good alternative suggestions. Even though we've all transcended onto this higher plane of mental abstractions, there is still value in showing your actual footwork. Where did your tool fall over? Why did you keep using it anyway?

I actually literally do this in a surprising social context. Otherwise, awkward dance floors. Specifically at weddings or oddly corporate events that have decided to have a dance floor. Basically, collections of people of very mixed abilities who don't know each other super well and yet are celebrating something vital together. I pride myself on understanding the assignment to look like I am enjoying myself in a way that invites other people in. I am very specifically not dancing like no one's watching. I am dancing like there's no downside to looking like a goon. I actually want people to see me and think, what a goon? That actually looks fun. Then I, as an enthusiastically mediocre dancer, will also have more fun because more people will be dancing. I also do this in socio-professional groups. I run a biweekly hallway track meeting for Photoshop developers where we just get together and talk off the record about our most recent formal meeting.

In a recent development, sometimes there's a lull in the conversation. I'll just jump in with an inane comment, sometimes a spicy question, just to let people know we aren't here trying to impress each other. I'll set the bar and then open the door and get out of the way because I love hearing experienced people hash things out. Being mediocre in public can invite people out with you. It brings out other intermediate-level folks. It brings out some shy experts because you've made it obvious that the bar for participation is one that they can easily clear. Now you're in a group of people sharing information and refining ideas before they've fully calcified, and you make each other better. Don't wait to be an expert to join a conversation about your tools. A caveat, when I tell people my advice to be joyfully imperfect in public, I usually mean it a little bit glibly.

Recent findings suggest that like in the sense of, but obviously not things that are core to your central identity. That would be terrible. No, like I can take up watercolors and show people that I'm an amusingly bad artist, or take up Chinese and let people laugh. When your skill at something is core to your identity, being mediocre in public is like doing a penance for a sin that you didn't even really get to enjoy committing. What I'm trying to do with every fiber of my being is to push this other skill, this meta skill of learning and adapting to change even deeper into my identity and recognizing that this squeaky, uncomfortable like, no, I'm terrible at this. It's like the lactic acid buildup the day after a workout. Is it comfortable? No, it sucks. It is the concrete feeling of getting better.

Some of you have been quietly bemused during this whole, here's how to not give up and survive section, because you are fully into learning the new thing. You are like, I am literally a core contributor on Gas Town, my good lady, what are you on about? This next section is for you. See, given the choice, I would rather dance than talk about the weather. I find it less awkward. Sorry, England. If I had absolute power, every awkward silence would just meld seamlessly into a dance break. Yet, I have not once committed the faux pas of grabbing some poor soul by the hand and dragging them onto the dance floor. I would never. Imagine this? You're sitting there at your linen-covered table trying to remember which wine was yours, and some absolute zealot comes and drags you by the hand onto the dance floor and then cheerfully bops away.

According to recent reports, you're welcome. It's not ok. Unless you very quickly find your own groove, as soon as you can get away with it, you will moonwalk right back to the table straight past both glasses of wine because this time you're choosing a table much farther from these diehards who keep trying to force you into places where you don't think you fit. People who are happy on the dance floor need to make it more obvious that this is a good place to be and not just keep shouting that all of the non-dance floor is lava and we're getting left behind. Another aspect of bringing people with you. A few months ago, I used an AI agent to help me initiative out decluttering my basement. I described the state of years of kid clutter accumulation, and listed off a couple sample starting ideas like disassembling the massive tower of cardboard box sculptures my kid had made, or sorting and condensing the various containers that were half full of miscellaneous.

According to recent reports, cursor came back with a useful blueprint and some excellent advice, which included, do not start with the miscellaneous bins. They will just exhaust you. Better to focus on low-decision weight, high-impact tasks. You all sighed with relief along there with me. Like, "Low-decision weight, high-impact? Yes, this plan will work. It's going to feel so good and productive." It did. I got the tower out. I got rid of expired food and old toiletries. I made so many easy decisions, and I wrapped up the day feeling tired but satisfied and a good day's work. Then I go to work the next day, and the AI agents are like, "Good, you're back. I saved all these high-decision weight tasks for you. You're welcome." It turns out I'm not the only one who's had this, hold up, I feel like I'm doing more work now. We're working harder. Birgitta mentioned this too.

We are tired. Please keep in mind that when you're telling people how great this tool is, it is not zero cost. It is free as in puppy. You can't just drop it on people's doorsteps. If you're walking around insisting that everyone adopts one, you've got to provide material support. One specific practice, Photoshop's strongest AI tooling advocates host weekly office hours. We're constantly re-explaining to each other how to export the right environment variables this week. The support is critical because you're asking people to work harder. If you're patient when you're asking someone if they've sourced their, Oh My Zsh config recently, they're more likely to keep trying your next, "You'll like this one, I promise." They're more likely to try that idea.

In a recent development, I know that some of you are very worried that some of us aren't fully embracing how different our jobs will be in five years. I actually said that to troll you a little because I know it's an order of magnitude faster. Remember that a source of denial can be a lack of certainty that we have the skills to deal with the change. The more you remind your teams and your colleagues that they have done hard things before, that they can learn and grow, that neuroplasticity is real, the more they can loosen their hold on denial. The more we all believe that we do have the skills to face it, the more likely we are to engage in real protective behaviors. My favorite researcher, Cat Hicks, again, if our teams have a culture of learning, we report more productivity. This next part is me, non-professional scientist, extrapolating, but I think if you have a choice between a team with one expert tool user and a team who believes that they can learn and has faith in the organizational support behind it, choose the team that identifies as learners, the team that thinks they can't use the tool yet.

According to recent reports, why are we here? This is a question whose spiritual pay grade is much higher than mine. I'm going to narrow it to something that I'm actually qualified to speak to, how did we get here? First, approximately one lifetime ago, a lot of people suffered through a lot of months of pregnancy. Some number of years ago, we went from not knowing technology to being paid to be good at it. Some number of weeks ago, we all decided it was a good use of three solid days of our time to sit at a tech conference, and then every single person got it together and left their home. If we had heads-up displays showing each of our logistical contortions we used to get here, we would be high-fiving and pouring each other pints all day. We all decided that, yes, it's worth it to take that skeptically optimistic next step to learn a new thing from a stranger rather than chatting up friends in the hall.

We've been through a lot to get here, and it's all been in the mad hope of finding that next good thing. We got here, and here and now is oddly harder than anything our industry has encountered, and even this is just a practice round for the next. The beginner's mindset that you're dusting off, the resilience that you did not want to have to shore up, and the communities that you're building now, this is not the last time you'll be calling on them. Latest Update: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Industry observers note that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

Industry observers note that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

In a recent development, that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

According to recent reports, you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Industry observers note that final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

Recent findings suggest that the gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

According to recent reports, an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

In a recent development, starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

In a recent development, table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

According to recent reports, only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Industry observers note that kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Recent findings suggest that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

It has been revealed that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

According to recent reports, this is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Sources indicate that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

Recent findings suggest that we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

According to recent reports, what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

Industry observers note that thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post highlights the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Sources indicate that each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

In a recent development, every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

In a recent development, at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Recent findings suggest that gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

According to recent reports, now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

Industry observers note that the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart.
  • Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.
  • Industry observers note that the patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart.

Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.

Industry observers note that the patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE).

Issued on November 25, the corrective update takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft.

According to recent reports, KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault.

In a recent development, good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved.

In a recent development, lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band update to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability.

Hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine.".

Industry observers note that avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®.

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • It has been revealed that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

It has been revealed that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

According to recent reports, arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

Sources indicate that we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

In a recent development, WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

According to recent reports, public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Sources indicate that falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Sources indicate that our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

Recent findings suggest that we thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

In a recent development, في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

Recent findings suggest that درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

Sources indicate that WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

It has been revealed that قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

According to recent reports, تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

In a recent development, سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

Industry observers note that يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

Industry observers note that يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

In a recent development, نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

📅 21 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blainehansen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis.
  • I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window).
  • But that's easier remarked than done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving, and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens newly introduced window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier remarked than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

In a recent development, it might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:.

Recent findings suggest that proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

Sources indicate that my chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a upcoming formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific proposal was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens newly introduced window):.

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:.

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens newly introduced window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

It has been revealed that I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

Stale links on UK public sector websites direct visitors to gambling dens

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.
  • UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.
  • The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.

UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.

The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.

LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative rolled out in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities.

Industry observers note that among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more.

Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa said: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous.".

The consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS.

The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes people to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – Newly introduced Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter.

The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP).

An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players.".

Recent findings suggest that the Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link.

All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment.

Recent findings suggest that digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content.

The findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed. ®.
