Breaking: Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Donsz

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0.
  • This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.
  • And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can promptly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.

In a recent development, the upcoming solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here, and here.

According to recent reports, my work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your firm could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team.

Recent findings suggest that on the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0. Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual upcoming subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero", referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one, that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Recent findings suggest that note: Chalk and the fresh trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

Sources indicate that but what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Industry observers note that some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type.

Industry observers note that notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

To check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

Recent findings suggest that prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:.

According to recent reports, A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy, String has the property Clone, And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

According to recent reports, finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't stated that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone, the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?-) are true!

In a recent development, the reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:.

Neither the newly introduced solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

Trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):.

In a recent development, we use type inference to determine that the type of the variable a is an integer. The same for b.

Having remarked that, sometimes during type inference we do have to ask things about traits, and will call into the trait solver. Furthermore, the trait solver sometimes "unifies type variables", which means that while Rust makes a query about traits, we might make some progress on figuring out what the types of some variables are.

In the example code, one place where the trait solver comes into effect is when we call weird_add. On the function there's a where bound. A where bound is a requirement that the Rust compiler must check before allowing a call to that function. In this case, Rust has to make sure that i32 (a type we found through type inference) implements the Add trait. To do that, the solver can use one of a couple of strategies, and we'll look at each. In this case, we'll be looking for an impl block that mentions the i32 type, and we'll find one of those in the standard library!

Industry observers note that once the trait solver finds this impl block, it acts as an answer to the question "does i32 implement Add?". We somtimes refer to this answer as a a proof that the statement holds.

The example code contains several more calls to the trait solver. One you may not have thought about is that all local variables in Rust have to implement the Sized trait to be allowed on the stack. The Sized trait codifies that the compiler knows how many bytes of memory the value takes up, so it can be allocated on the stack. So, there will also be a query to the trait solver asking "does i32 implement Sized?".

The proof for this statement doesn't come from an impl block though. I did say that the compiler has several stratagies to derive proofs. In this case, the fact that some primitive types implement Sized is built-in to the compiler. i32 is inherently Sized, and there is no impl block anywhere that states so.

In a recent development, answering Sized queries in general turns out to be quite hard because of the shear volume at which it occurs. To compile rust's standard library, we'll ask "does type implement Sized?" about 800 000 times! Additionally, answering it isn't always this simple. Let's take a slightly more involved example:.

It has been revealed that to prove Kitten: Sized, a recursive process takes place. Both fields have to implement Sized too. So in the process of answering this question, the trait solver will produce more questions to be answered. Kitten: Sized leads to String: Sized & f64: Sized. f64 luckily is trivial again, and built into the compiler. String isn't though, and we go one more layer deeper to Vec: Sized, etcetera.

In Rust, generic functions can be type checked standalone. The example using weird_add doesn't need a main function to be checked, and may emit its own type errors.

This is where the trait solver actually does the most work. For example, to type check weird_add, we have to prove that a + b is valid. a + b desugars to a.add(b), and when finding the method add the trait solver gets invoked, since the add method comes from the Add trait.

According to recent reports, previously, proof candidates came either from impl blocks or they were built into the compiler. Not here though! A fresh proof strategy is used here instead. When calling weird_add we saw that a where bound acts as a requirement that has to be checked before calling, but that means that inside weird_add we can assume that where bound holds and thus it acts as a proof strategy. Concretely, we know a has the type T, and to answer the question "does T implement Add" we find a where bound that notes so.

According to recent reports, add isn't the only trait bound that has to be proven inside weird_add. This is another place where we have to prove that T: Sized. Again we have to look for candidates, and there's no built in one for generic types T, nor is there an impl block, nor a where bound that mentions Sized. So how does that work? Well, it turns out the where bound is implicit. T: Add really means T: Add + Sized, and so proving Sized works the same as proving Add.

On lobsters I got asked about whether the Add bound is required to add the Sized bound. The T: Sized implicit bound gets added for any generic. Even if there was not already an Add bound, T would still be Sized. Right now, you can opt out of that implicit bound using T: ?Sized (or in the example, T: Add + ?Sized). In the future we may change the syntax for that to T: MetaSized. Look for the keyword "Sized Hierarchy" if you want to learn more. This document should also give you a primer.

In a recent development, finally, this code will actually give a type error, because there's one more trait to prove. Because b gets mentioned twice, we have to clone or copy values of type T. The function signature really should have been:.

To summarize, trait solving is the process of answering questions about relations between types and traits. These questions are submitted to the trait solver, and the trait solver looks for candidates in the form of:.

When it finds one of these, we say we've found a proof, and if we cannot find one, a type error is emitted.

It has been revealed that sofar, all trait solving came down to finding a single candidate, but that's not always how it works. Let's look at the definition of the From and the Into traits:.

If the trait solver gets a question like u32: Into (does u32 implement the Into trait), it will find the impl block above. However, the impl block is generic, and has a where bound that claims "T implements Into U IF U implements From T". Luckily there's another impl block that gives that implementation and so the initial statement can be proven.

What this all means, is that while answering a question, the trait solver emits more questions. These subquestions get added to an internal queue in the trait solver, and this queue of questions will be proven one after the other. Like this, some questions can turn into several subquestions, which can even have their own subquestions again.

It has been revealed that also, in the example from above, the second question actually has two proofs! There are two impl blocks that apply, since there's also this blanket implementation for identity conversion:.

In a recent development, some preference takes place here. Since this is a blanket implementation, the other more specific one takes precedence. We can think about the trait solving about answering a tree of candidates that may apply. In this case, the single candidate for u32: Into turns into two, u64: From and T: From.

Something we'll not cover today, but this tree of candidates in reality is not a tree, it can have cycles! This has been the cause of both many bugs, and many rust compiler developers' nightmares.

The trait solver doesn't just deal with traits. An important thing it has to also consider is the associated types of traits. Let's look at the Add trait:.

An implementation of the Add trait can decide what the Output type will be equal to. Remember the definition of Add for integers?

It states that when you add two i32s, we get back an i32. The reason the trait solver cares about associated types is that sometimes answering questions creates subquestions that mention associated types.

Because we wrote Output = T, the trait solver has to check that the candidate impl block has an Output type that's equal to T. We could've also written a more general function signature to something like:.

Or really to make it works you have to go one step further (click to expand).

According to recent reports, hold on! impl blocks can define inputs they act on, like impl Foo for i32 applies when the input is i32. It can make these inputs variables, like impl Foo for T. And impl blocks can also define outputs thrugh associated types.

Recent findings suggest that what we've done here, is make impl blocks powerful enough to act as functions, with inputs and outputs. And Alonzo Church proved that a language with only pure functions is in fact turing complete.

This is why Prolog is a fully-fledged turing complete programming language, and so is Rust's type system. People have defined numbers completely in Rust's type system in a crate called typenum, and have gone even further by implementing a chess engine inside the type system.

Trait solving ends up being a subsystem that the compiler spends quite a large portion of its time in. In general, there are two reasons for that:.

In a recent development, this ends up replacing the trait solver more complicated than you might think. People have already written many programs using the old solver, and because the fresh solver internally makes different assumptions (sometimes in the name of soundness, remember the old solver has many bugs), we end up having programs that take both longer and shorter to compile. Sometimes with a polynomial factor, sometimes even with an exponential factor.

For example, the crate unic-ucd contains code along the lines of:.

Sources indicate that it lists a whole bunch of unicode characters, and each constant inside these slices are themselves string literals. That means each of them has an associated lifetime variable, that at some point gets inferred to 'static since we're assigning to a const. Now the upcoming trait solver, in some cases where the old solver did not, reasons about lifetimes.

Recent findings suggest that now sometimes, the rust compiler attempts see if two types are equal. This process may have side effects, in that it may make some progress towards inferring other types in the program. Because these side effects are sometimes undesireable, we have a system to "attempt" to unify types, and then roll back the results. To be able to do rollbacks we sometimes keep a trace of all operations we perform, so we can run them in reverse to get back to where we started. However, sometimes this tracking is more expensive than simply making a copy of the state and putting that copy back.

According to recent reports, in this case, during borrow checking, we call into the the trait solver and end up unifying two "lifetime variables", which we roll back. This specific rollback involves a copy, though there was a shortcut. We keep track of a single boolean: "was any lifetime variable modified". If none were, the rollback can be skipped. The old solver wouldn't do such unifications, so the rollback could always be skipped, while in the latest solver we couldn't do so.

According to recent reports, often, there are very few lifetime variables in scope, so doing a rollback isn't so bad. However, the example above lists every unicode character in existence, so the list is rather long. And for every item in the list, we'd do such a rollback, that copied all lifetime variables (for which there is one per element in the list). So N undos copying a list of N lifetime variables, that's a quadratic factor! So this crate would compile just fine with the old solver, and be 200 times slower with the newly introduced solver. Oops!

There are two important strategies we use to make the trait solver faster. First of all, there's caching, and a lot of it. For example, in the following example we prove that i32: Sized three times:.

We'd like to make it so we only need to figure out whether a specific type is Sized once, and so we cache the result.

It has been revealed that the second optimization we use a lot is not caching funnily enough. Accessing the cache can be rather expensive (we'll get to why). So in this case, since i32 is trivially Sized, we can answer the question faster by never looking in the cache. For more complicated types this is not true.

A naive cache would be a mapping from questions asked to the trait solver, to answers (errors or proofs). So, something like HashMap, but this wouldn't perform so well. Let's look at this example:.

Here we've renamed the variables T and U between foo and bar. We'll prove two question, that T: Into and later U: Into. Because of the renamings these two proofs are the same, but the questions are technically different. If we don't do something about variable renaming, we'd have cache misses all the time.

It has been revealed that another issue is that this cache wouldn't even work. By now, we've learned that candidates for proofs can come from three sources:.

Industry observers note that the first two play nicely, because the same impl blocks and compiler built-ins are around for all questions submitted to the trait solver. Howver, where bounds are different for every function, and thus a proof that a type implements a trait inside of one function, may not be reusable inside another function.

Recent findings suggest that in the example above, we prove that T: Into twice. Inside foo that's ok, but not inside of bar. So if we naively cached that T: Into we wouldn't notice that bar is incorrect.

Industry observers note that we call the set of bounds that are in-scope during trait solving the ParamEnv (parameter environment), and so the cache would really have to look like HashMap<(ParamEnv, Question), Answer>. Since for every function, the ParamEnv is different, we'd have even more cache misses.

To improve our chances of a cache hit, we perform a process called "Canonicalization". During canonicalization, we do two things. First we'll rename all variables with numbers. So, T: Into will become ?0: Into (variable 0 implements Into variable 1). Since this process is consistent, another renamed input like U: Into also gets this numbering and is compatible.

In addition, we'll try very hard to figure out which where bounds in the ParamEnv actually matter. If there are bounds that won't affect the result of the query, we can avoid putting them in the cache key, making cache hits more likely.

So, in the rust compiler, the cache really looks more like a HashMap<(Paramenv, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer> Note that the answer of every query now has to be de-canonicalized. We call this "instantiation". When we turn T: Into into ?0: Into, and cache its result, and we later look for U: Into, we have to turn the answer (that mentions variables 0 and 1) into U and T respectively. In other words, by canonicalizing we make cache hits much more likely, but the process isn't free. Hence not caching is sometimes worth it for simple questions.

Now is this worth it? Below I've plotted the hit rate of the fresh solver's cache for various popular crates, and one internal rust compiler benchmark.

In a recent development, as you can see, we can often avoid almost 80% of all trait solving by caching. The last two bars are for a crate called wg-grammar. It is a crate that used to be particularly slow with the new trait solver. Part of my job this year used to be specifically optimizing it.

Sources indicate that the problem was that there's one more property that has to be part of the cache key: which opaque types are in scope. An opaque type is a type you write as a "return position impl trait". For example:.

foo returns impl IntoIterator. By doing so, callers of this function don't get to know what specific type is returned. Only that they can iterate over whatever they get back. Inside of this function foo, the trait solver will infer which specific type gets returned (a Vec), but in other functions calling foo, this information is not available. So, this is another piece of information that may affect answers from function to function, just like the ParamEnv.

So, the real cache has one more input: HashMap<(ParamEnv, OpaqueTypes, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer>. What that really means is that the following two functions both submit the question i32: Clone to the trait solver, but cannot reuse the cache entry:.

This ends up mattering a lot in async code, or code like parser-generators that tend to return -> impl Parser from functions. That's unfortunate, because the fact that opaque types are different ends up almost never affecting the outcome of a question. Sure, we can come up with examples where it does, but in practice it almost never does.

It has been revealed that so, the fix here is to remove opaque types from the cache key to the cached value like so: HashMap<(ParamEnv, CanonicalQuestion), (CanonicalAnswer, OpaqueTypeState)>. Then, every time we answer a question that may be different because of opaque types, we record in the opaque type state under what condition it may affect the answer, and continue assuming the answer is unaffected (this is often the case). Then, when we get a cached answer in a specific environment, we look at the opaque type state, to see whether the answer might be affected by current context. It almost never is, but if it ends up mattering, we retry the question but now no longer assuming opaque types don't matter.

It has been revealed that this sometimes makes performance worse (we sometimes do double work), but since its so rare, we get an improvement over all by having more cache hits. In the graph from above, there are two bars for wg-grammar. One where the hit rate is 73% and one where the hit rate is 79%. This 6% difference translates to some the wg-grammar crate first taking 28 seconds to compile, and afterwards only 14 seconds. That's 2x faster!

(click to expand for me going into a little more detail about this).

Sources indicate that technically even when we use opaque type tracking, the list of opaques is still part of the key. We just set it to be an empty list. That means that in the rerun, we un-empty it and we get a different cache key. Now because we keep the cache entry with the empty list around too, when a newly introduced query comes along it will also empty the list, find a cache hit that matches this empty list but with tracking information (so it's not redoing work getting that tracking). Then, if it decides it needs to rerun, it adds back the list of opaques and could totally get a cache hit again if we've tried with those exact opaques before.

Of note is also that sometimes we run multiple dependent queries without their opaques like this. We can only un-empty the list once we get back up to the root at the point where we emptied the list to see if they may be unnecessary. To make sure we don't spend too much time running giant query trees we have a bailing mechanism built in to the tracking. Once a query and it's dependencies try to access opaques more than 3 times (or when they do so in very specific ways) we assume that it's unlikely for opaques not to influence the outcome of the query in any way, and we bail out of the "erased" attempts (recording in each dependent result that it's likely a rerun is necessary) and rerun without every knowing the original (erased) result, since it's unlikely to be correct. Future queries will see that this happened in the tracking information, and never attempt to erase opaque types. They know that the attempt is likely wasted.

Now there's an even more subtle thing going on. Sometimes assuming that opaques are empty (in a specific path related to coroutines) leads to query cycles. So, in that case we are forced to do this bailing and to rerun with opaque types even if the answer would've maybe been correct with the erased environment, because the compiler would crash if it encountered the cycle and we want to avoid those at all costs. In this case we may end up rerunning with opaque types, get to the exact same point, and continue to return the exact same result as we would have when we erased the environment previously. This is sadly unavoidable.

This, and more optimizations meant that wg-grammar used to take almost 200 Billion cpu cycles to compile, and now only about 7 Billion.

Now this is my second blog post about trait solver optimization. The other one is a little more technical, and goes into all the different things we did over the past year to bring the new trait solver towards stabilization. Go read it next if you're interested, and thank you for reading! If you're still interested in learning more about this, I'm happy to answer any questions if you reach out.

It has been revealed that also, hell yea! you made it to the end. Here's my cat.

Breaking: 'Significant number of customer records' pwned in Flight Centre Travel Group breach

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (473 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally.
  • Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) states "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.
  • The Brisbane-headquartered organization remarked the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally.

Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) states "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.

The Brisbane-headquartered organization remarked the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.

Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.

Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

In a recent development, an initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.

Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company stated.

It has been revealed that "FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes.".

Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.

The tech giant noted it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their prepares.

Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.

The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.

More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.

Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.

Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, mentioned attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Sources indicate that speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel remarked: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or promptly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

"Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

It has been revealed that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

According to recent reports, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 demonstrates strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Industry observers note that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Sources indicate that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Sources indicate that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

In a recent development, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team unveiled the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

  • We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.
  • Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
  • Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.

Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.

Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Sources indicate that edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment.".

Recent findings suggest that that investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to.".

The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

In a recent development, monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.

The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Industry observers note that its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a newly introduced board-led governance model.

The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.

"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," stated DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.

Recent findings suggest that the watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • In a recent development, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

In a recent development, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Recent findings suggest that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Sources indicate that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

Recent findings suggest that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

It has been revealed that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Recent findings suggest that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Industry observers note that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

According to recent reports, every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Proposal for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

In a recent development, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Sources indicate that beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

According to recent reports, launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Industry observers note that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

It has been revealed that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

Recent findings suggest that on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Industry observers note that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

According to recent reports, * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

According to recent reports, † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can patch the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the fresh weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

Sources indicate that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Sources indicate that update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Recent findings suggest that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one patch behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

In a recent development, we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

According to recent reports, we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

According to recent reports, we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

It has been revealed that our score-versus-latency plot demonstrates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

According to recent reports, decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

Industry observers note that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

Recent findings suggest that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Industry observers note that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

According to recent reports, that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Sources indicate that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR After Three-Year Migration.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.

Written by Primer engineers Josh Black and Marie Lucca, the post explains how component counts on certain pages began to explode in 2023, exposing scaling problems with the existing styled-components setup. Initial page loads, server render times and style update costs all grew with component count. The team picked CSS Modules because it kept native CSS features and co-location while removing client and server runtime work, letting styles roll up into static stylesheets delivered with the HTML.

In a recent development, for every Primer component the team added a CSS Modules variant, gated it behind a feature flag, verified parity with visual regression tests, then rolled it out from the Primer team to GitHub staff and finally all owners. By December 2024, Primer itself was fully on CSS Modules. The harder half was the roughly 7,760 sx prop usages scattered across github.com, the de facto styling standard for years. A transitional @primer/styled-react package let sx keep working against migrated components during the crossover.

A typical conversion looks like this:.

A rotation of eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, seeing SSR improvements ranging from 3% up to 22% per page. The final 895 props were cleared in three weeks by two engineers leaning heavily on Copilot coding agents. GitHub also had to decouple theming for its seven themes and high-contrast variants before pulling styled-components out entirely. A VS Code plugin and internal codemod cut the manual burden, and GitHub notes that styled-components entering maintenance mode reinforced the direction.

On Hacker News one commenter running a similar migration reported a 30% build time speed improvement and much better tree shaking on Next.js across a codebase over 1M lines. Others were sceptical about user impact, with one arguing that the reduction in size was not massive enough to justify making all CSS names unreadable, adding that hashed class names make ad-blockers, custom CSS and browser extensions harder to build. A separate thread noted that CSS-in-JS can be made zero-runtime without moving to Modules at all.

Sources indicate that gitHub joins a broader shift away from runtime CSS-in-JS. Linear recently completed its own 1,000-PR move from styled-components to Meta's atomic StyleX library, citing similar render-time concerns after upgrading to React 18's concurrent mode. Others using vanilla-extract or Tailwind have shifted style generation to build time entirely. The common thread is to pay the cost once at build, not on every request.

In a recent development, the Primer Design System is GitHub's open-source component library, providing the foundational building blocks used across github.com. Teams following the same path can start from the Primer React v38 release notes and the migration guide for CSS variables, which covers the move from sx props to CSS Modules.

Tech's outage problem needs maintenance, not conspiracy theories

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forrester warns that shiny new services rest on brittle systems as organizations skimp on resilience.
  • Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.
  • The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forrester warns that shiny new services rest on brittle systems as organizations skimp on resilience.

Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.

The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.

The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester remarked.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations.".

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it.".

According to recent reports, earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

According to recent reports, in October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.

In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Industry observers note that aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.

It has been revealed that "Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report mentioned.

Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

In a recent development, "Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund fresh customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate.".

Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®.
